big_idea: A revision lesson for the gap between finishing 9A and Test 1: a short video, four gap-fill passages, exam technique and a plan for your own revision.
goals: I can use the correct key words to complete passages on variation, inheritance, adaptation and natural selection.
I can say which parts of 9A I am confident about and which I need to revise before Test 1.

keywords.meaning: a physical (non-living) part of the environment, e.g. temperature
the activities of other organisms, e.g. predation, disease
the differences between the characteristics of organisms
differences in characteristics that are passed on from parents to offspring
a section of DNA that carries the instructions for one characteristic
when a male gamete and a female gamete fuse (join together)
a characteristic that helps an organism survive in its habitat
a species with no living members left
when organisms need the same limited resource, e.g. food or light
organisms better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their genes
a change over time in the characteristics of organisms, sometimes making a new species

card_flow: Do Now: key word brain dump
Watch a short video on natural selection
Four gap-fill rounds: fill, then check in green pen
Exam skills and your revision plan
misconceptions: Students fill the gaps by matching the first word they see in the box. Read the whole sentence first, then choose.
Organisms change themselves to suit the environment. Natural selection works on inherited variation that is already in the population; the moths did not change colour.
Environmental variation (a scar, a suntan) is passed on. It is not; only genes are inherited.
"Only a theory" means evolution is a guess. A scientific theory has been tested many times and is supported by a great deal of evidence.
equipment: Revision cards (A6, four to an A4 sheet) or the A4 worksheet, English or CN version, one per student
Projector and speakers, with the video opened and tested before the lesson

slides.subtitle: Revise 9A before Test 1: a video, four gap-fill passages and a plan for your revision
slides.notes: A single revision lesson for the gap between finishing 9A and Test 1. It covers the four 9A lessons taught: 1, 2, 6 and 7. It also works as a cover lesson: the slides carry the instructions and the notes say what to do. Print the cards (A6, four to an A4 sheet) or the A4 worksheet, English or CN version. Open and test the video before the lesson.

slides.title: Do Now: key word brain dump
prompt: Two minutes, in your book: write down every 9A key word you can remember.
1. Which key words are about variation and the environment?
2. Which key words are about genes and inheritance?
3. Which key words are about adaptation and extinction?
4. Which key words are about natural selection and evolution?
slides.notes: Two minutes of silent writing, then a minute to share. Do not reveal the words: the passages that follow do that. Useful words to listen for: environment, abiotic, biotic, variation, gene, gamete, adaptation, extinct, competition, natural selection, evolution.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read the goals. Explain the rhythm: four rounds, two minutes to fill a passage and one minute to check it in green pen. Remind students to read the whole sentence before they choose a word from the box.

slides.title: Watch: how does natural selection work?
slides.heading: Natural selection
slides.instruction: Tick each key word when you hear it. Then write one thing you did not know.
slides.backup: A shorter option: Khan Academy, "Natural selection in peppered moths" (3 min 17 s). Stop it before the end if Test 1 has not been sat.

(2) Khan Academy, Natural selection in peppered moths, 3 min 17 s, on YouTube: the best fit for a short slot, but its last part is about pale moths returning as pollution fell, which is the scenario in Test 1 question 6, so stop it before that if the test has not been sat. slides.title: If the video will not play: the peppered moth in four steps
text: Variation: a few moths had genes that made them black.
The environment changed: soot made the trees black.
Birds spotted and ate more pale moths. More black moths survived and reproduced, passing on their genes.
Each generation had more black moths. The environment "selected" the black variation.
slides.key_idea: Natural selection: the environment selects the inherited variations that survive and are passed on.
slides.notes: Use this slide as the video if the clip will not play, or as the recap straight after it. Read the four steps aloud and let students tick the key words on their While You Watch card as they hear them.

slides.title: The four rounds
steps: Round 1: variation and the environment. Round 2: inherited variation.
Round 3: adaptation and extinction. Round 4: natural selection and evolution.
Two minutes: read each whole sentence, then fill the gap with a word from the box. Use each word once.
One minute: check on the screen. Mark in green pen and correct any gap you missed.
Finished early? Start Stretch (no word box) or Challenge (write your own gap fill).
slides.footer: Read the whole sentence first. The word that fits the meaning is the answer, not the first word in the box.
slides.notes: Run the rounds with a visible timer. Between rounds, put up the answer slide. Praise correcting in green pen.

slides.title: Round 1 answers: variation and the environment
lines: The surroundings of an organism are its **environment**.
Non-living factors, such as temperature and light, are **abiotic** factors.
Disease and predation come from living things, so they are **biotic** factors.
A feature of an organism, such as its height, is a **characteristic**.
A scar is caused by the surroundings, so it is **environmental** variation and not inherited.
Height can have any value in a range, so it is **continuous** variation.
Blood group has only a few possible values, so it is **discontinuous** variation.
A **species** is a group that can breed together to produce offspring that can breed.
slides.notes: Answers: environment, abiotic, biotic, characteristic, environmental, continuous, discontinuous, species. Most common slips: environment and environmental swapped in round 1; genes and gene mixed up in rounds 2 to 4.

slides.title: Round 2 answers: inherited variation
lines: Differences passed on from parents to offspring are **inherited** variation.
Genetic information is stored in the **nucleus** of every cell.
A section of DNA that carries instructions for one characteristic is a **gene**.
Sperm cells and egg cells are sex cells called **gametes**.
A male gamete and a female gamete join together at **fertilisation**.
The fertilised egg cell is called a **zygote**.
Each gamete carries different genes, so brothers and sisters are not **identical**.
Grouped continuous data give a bell-shaped chart: a **normal** distribution.
slides.notes: Answers: inherited, nucleus, gene, gametes, fertilisation, zygote, identical, normal. Most common slips: environment and environmental swapped in round 1; genes and gene mixed up in rounds 2 to 4.

slides.title: Round 3 answers: adaptation and extinction
lines: A feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat is an **adaptation**.
Adaptations come from an organism's **genes**, so it cannot change them.
If a species is in danger of dying out, it is **endangered**.
A species with no living members left is **extinct**.
Organisms needing the same limited resource, such as food, are in **competition**.
A species found naturally in a place, such as the UK red squirrel, is **native**.
The number of different species in an area is its **biodiversity**.
Nature reserves, **breeding** programmes and gene banks protect biodiversity.
slides.notes: Answers: adaptation, genes, endangered, extinct, competition, native, biodiversity, breeding. Most common slips: environment and environmental swapped in round 1; genes and gene mixed up in rounds 2 to 4.

slides.title: Round 4 answers: natural selection and evolution
lines: A few peppered moths had **genes** that made them black; most were pale.
Soot blackened the trees, so the black moths were better **camouflaged**.
Birds ate more pale moths, so more black moths survived and **reproduced**.
They passed on their genes, so the next **generation** had more black moths.
The environment selected the helpful variation. This is natural **selection**.
A change over time in the characteristics of organisms is **evolution**.
A new **species** can form if two populations can no longer breed together.
An idea tested many times and supported by evidence is a scientific **theory**.
slides.notes: Answers: genes, camouflaged, reproduced, generation, selection, evolution, species, theory. Most common slips: environment and environmental swapped in round 1; genes and gene mixed up in rounds 2 to 4.

slides.title: Before the test: how to earn the marks
text: Look at the marks. One mark is one point, so a 2-mark answer needs two points.
State or Give: a short answer. No reason is needed.
Describe: say what happens. Explain: say what happens and why, using the word "because".
Use the key words. Write "genes", "survive" and "reproduce", not "it changed to survive".
slides.key_idea: Read the whole question, circle the command word and check the marks before you write.
slides.notes: Two minutes only. The command words are on the CN worksheet with Chinese. Point out that Test 1 questions show the marks in brackets, like [2].

slides.title: Plan your revision
steps: On your confidence card, colour each statement: red (not sure), amber (nearly) or green (confident).
Find them in the revision guide: section 1 environmental variation, 2 inherited variation, 3 adaptation and extinction, 4 natural selection and evolution.
At home, do the Test yourself questions for those two sections and mark them with the answers at the back.
slides.footer: Test 1 has biology, chemistry and physics parts. This lesson prepares you for the biology part.
slides.notes: Ask students to be honest: red is useful, not a failure. Walk round and ask two students which sections they will revise. Check the revision guide section numbers are right for the version they have.

slides.title: Teach it back
slides.prompt: Tell your partner the peppered moth story in one or two sentences. Use at least five key words.
frames: A few moths had ___ that made them black, but most were pale.
More ___ moths survived and ___, so the next ___ had more of them.
slides.notes: Then ask each student to write, in any language, the one key word they most need to practise. Collect two or three to revisit next lesson.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: Differences between organisms of the same species are called ______.
Organisms that are better adapted are more likely to ______ and reproduce.
A change over time in the characteristics of organisms is called ______.
slides.instruction: On your exit ticket card or worksheet strip. Complete each sentence with no word box. Work alone.

slides.title: What we revised in 9A
slides.next: Test 1. Use the revision guide, sections 1 to 4 (biology), and the Test yourself questions.
points: Variation can be environmental (not inherited) or inherited (genes from two gametes joining at fertilisation).
Adaptations come from genes; when the environment changes a species can become endangered or extinct.
Natural selection: the environment selects the inherited variations that survive and reproduce, generation after generation.
Evolution is a change over time in the characteristics of organisms, and it can produce new species.
slides.notes: Point students to the revision guide: section 1 (environmental variation), 2 (inherited variation), 3 (adaptation and extinction), 4 (natural selection and evolution).

filled.title: Stretch: Grey and red squirrels
lines: Grey squirrels were brought to the UK from the USA in the 1870s.
Greys and reds are in **competition** for the same food, such as acorns.
Greys can digest unripe acorns, so they eat the acorns **first**.
Greys carry squirrel pox, which **kills** red squirrels but not greys.
Greys store more fat, so more of them **survive** a long winter.
So greys are better **adapted** in many woods, and red squirrels have become **rare**.
Reds still do well in **conifer** forests, because their light bodies suit thin branches.
Which species is better adapted depends on the **habitat**.
